meta.title: Who really said "Being entirely honest with oneself is a good exercise"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Freud wrote it to Wilhelm Fliess on 15 October 1897, in the letter that first described the Oedipus complex. The wording is the 1954 translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Being entirely honest with oneself is a good exercise'?
meta.ogDescription: Freud really wrote it — to Wilhelm Fliess, 15 October 1897. The famous English phrasing comes from the 1954 Mosbacher–Strachey translation.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Freud wrote it in a private letter to his friend Wilhelm Fliess on 15 October 1897 — the letter in which he first described being “in love with my mother and jealous of my father.” The familiar English wording is the 1954 translation published as The Origins of Psycho-Analysis; Jeffrey Moussaieff Masson’s 1985 complete edition renders the same sentence “Being totally honest with oneself is a good exercise.”

source.excerpt: Being entirely honest with oneself is a good exercise. One idea of general value has occurred to me…
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ lists the line under the 1890s and cites it to a “Letter to Wilhelm Fliess (15 October 1897), as quoted in Origins of Psychoanalysis” — a dated primary document, not a floating attribution.

The letter checks out independently. Masson’s 1985 translation of the 15 October 1897 letter ↗ contains the same sentence as “Being totally honest with oneself is a good exercise,” in a letter about Freud’s self-analysis that goes on to the mother/father passage. Two independent translations of one letter, one sentence.

The edition behind the famous wording is The origins of psycho-analysis; letters to Wilhelm Fliess, drafts and notes, 1887-1902, Basic Books, 1954 ↗; a contemporary review ↗ records it as the “authorised translation by Eric Mosbacher and James Strachey.”

The German original came first: Wellcome Collection’s catalogue ↗ records Aus den Anfängen der Psychoanalyse: Briefe an Wilhelm Fliess, Abhandlungen und Notizen aus den Jahren 1887-1902, Imago Pub. Co., London, [1950].
source.excerptNote: The opening sentence is the wording Wikiquote cites to Origins of Psychoanalysis ↗; the continuation is as quoted in George Steiner’s Nostalgia for the Absolute. In Masson’s 1985 translation ↗ the same letter opens “My self-analysis is in fact the most essential thing I have at present” and renders the honesty line with “totally” in place of “entirely.”

source.rightsNote: Freud wrote the letter in 1897, but a letter is not published by being written. It first appeared in print in 1950 in German ↗ and in 1954 in English — both well after the 1931 United States public-domain cut-off — so the letter as published and the English translation are each treated here as in copyright. The English sentence people share is separately the translators’ work.

author.name: Sigmund Freud
author.heading: Sigmund Freud
author.bio: Sigmund Freud (6 May 1856 – 23 September 1939) was, in Wikipedia’s summary, “an Austrian neurologist and the founder of psychoanalysis.” After his father died in 1896 he fell into a spell of heart irregularities, disturbing dreams and depression that prompted a self-analysis of his own dreams and childhood memories — the private project that produced this sentence. Through those years his sounding board was the Berlin physician Wilhelm Fliess (1858–1928), whom he had met in 1887 and with whom he kept up the extensive correspondence that charts psychoanalysis in its earliest, unguarded form.

misattribution.heading: The name is right. The words are a translator's.
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare famous-name quotes that survives inspection: Freud really wrote it, on a date we can name. What does not survive inspection is the idea that these are his words in any literal sense, or that he meant them as a standalone maxim.

items.why: Freud wrote in German. “Being entirely honest with oneself is a good exercise” is the English of the 1954 edition — the “authorised translation by Eric Mosbacher and James Strachey” ↗. No quote site that reprints it says so.

Masson’s complete edition of the correspondence translates the same sentence as “Being totally honest with oneself is a good exercise” ↗. Both are faithful; neither is Freud’s own English, because there wasn’t one.

Reprinted as a free-floating life lesson. In the letter it is a preface — Freud steadying himself before telling Fliess he had found in his own case “being in love with my mother and jealous of my father” ↗. The honesty he is recommending is a specific and uncomfortable one.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: genuinely Freud, from his letter to Wilhelm Fliess of 15 October 1897, cited in Wikiquote’s sourced section to Origins of Psychoanalysis ↗ — but the English sentence is a 1954 translator’s, and the letter it comes from is anything but a motivational poster.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Freud wrote this line in the year after his father’s death, in the middle of the self-analysis that Wikipedia describes as prompted by the heart irregularities, disturbing dreams and depression that followed that loss. The letter opens with him telling Fliess that the self-analysis is “the most essential thing I have at present.”

The sentence about honesty is not a self-help maxim — it is Freud bracing himself. Immediately after it comes the admission that made him famous: that he had found in his own case the phenomenon of being in love with his mother and jealous of his father, and now considered it a universal event in early childhood. What we quote as a tidy aphorism is the throat-clearing before the most consequential confession in the history of psychoanalysis.
context.detailsSummary: How a letter Freud wanted destroyed came to be published
detailsBody: Freud ordered that his correspondence with Fliess be destroyed. Wikipedia’s account is blunt: the correspondence “is known today only because Marie Bonaparte purchased Freud’s letters to Fliess and refused to permit their destruction.”

The rescued letters first reached print in German in 1950, as Aus den Anfängen der Psychoanalyse: Briefe an Wilhelm Fliess, Abhandlungen und Notizen aus den Jahren 1887–1902 (Imago Publishing Co., London), edited by Marie Bonaparte, Anna Freud and Ernst Kris. The English translation by Eric Mosbacher and James Strachey followed in 1954. That publication history is why this 1897 sentence is still under copyright — and why the version everyone shares is a translator’s English, not Freud’s German.
context.pull: My self-analysis is in fact the most essential thing I have at present.
